Core Strengthening for Back Pain

A static, spine-sparing core programme built on holds rather than sit-ups — plus the daily habits that decide whether back pain keeps coming back.

Most back pain is not caused by anything that shows up on a scan, and most of it settles. The problem is that it comes back — and what decides whether it comes back is largely how the trunk muscles behave during ordinary movements: getting out of the car, lifting a grandchild, loading the dishwasher, carrying shopping on one side.

The programme below trains the trunk to stay still and stiff while the arms and legs do the moving. That is the job the back muscles actually have. It deliberately avoids sit-ups, crunches and repeated bending, because those train the opposite thing.

Why I do not give patients sit-ups

A sit-up bends the lumbar spine under load, dozens of times per set, which is the loading pattern that damages discs in laboratory testing. It also pulls hard on the psoas muscle, which compresses the lower back. There is a better way to train the same muscles: hold the trunk still and let the limbs move. That is what every exercise here does.

How to use this sheet
  • Read it once through, then start with the first two or three exercises only.
  • Add an exercise every week or two rather than starting everything at once.
  • Print it, tick off the days, and bring it back to your appointment.
  • This sheet is general information for my patients. If you have been given different, specific advice about your own condition, that advice comes first.

Four things worth understanding first

They explain why this programme looks so different from the abdominal workouts people expect.

⏱️ Endurance beats strength

Healthy backs are not distinguished by powerful trunk muscles but by trunk muscles that can hold on for a long time without tiring. That is why every exercise here is a short hold repeated many times, rather than a maximal effort.

🧱 Stiffness is protection

The spine is stable when the muscles around it stiffen together, like guy ropes on a mast. That skill — bracing — is what transfers to real life, and it is why the first exercise on this page is not an exercise at all but a technique.

🌅 Mornings are different

The discs absorb fluid overnight and are at their most swollen and least tolerant of bending in the first hour after you get up. Save the floor exercises, and any heavy lifting or toe-touching, until you have been up and about for an hour.

🚶 Motion is the medicine

The single most useful thing you can do for a back that keeps flaring is to walk regularly. Bed rest, once standard advice, is now known to make back pain worse and to prolong it.

Hurt is not harm — and this is central to back pain

Muscles that have worked will ache. As a rule of thumb, discomfort up to about 4 or 5 out of 10 during and after exercise is acceptable, provided it settles back to your normal level within 24 hours and is not getting worse week on week. Sharp, sudden or one-sided pain is a reason to stop.

Step 1 — Learn the skill

One week. Everything else depends on it.

Learning to brace (do this first)

10 × 10-second braces, once or twice a day for the first week
Technique, not a workout

Every core exercise on this sheet depends on this one skill: stiffening the trunk without holding your breath and without flattening your back into the floor.

  1. Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
  2. Put your fingertips on the muscles just inside your hip bones.
  3. Imagine someone is about to poke you in the stomach, and stiffen your whole abdominal wall against it — a firm, all-round tension, about 20–30% of your maximum. You should feel the muscles under your fingers tighten.
  4. Do not suck your stomach in, and do not push your low back flat against the floor. The natural small hollow in your low back should stay.
  5. Keep breathing normally while you hold it. Say your address out loud to prove you are not holding your breath.
  6. Hold 10 seconds, relax 5 seconds, repeat 10 times.
Make it harderPractise bracing while sitting, standing, and while getting out of a chair — this is where it actually protects you.
Make it easierIf you cannot brace and breathe at the same time, drop the effort to 10% and just practise the breathing.
SafetyBreath-holding raises blood pressure. If you have heart disease or aneurysm, keep the effort light and the breathing continuous.
Why it worksBracing (all-round stiffening) rather than hollowing (drawing the belly in) is what generates spine stability under real-world loads. The two approaches have been argued over for twenty years; bracing is the more robust skill for daily activity.

Step 2 — The three core exercises

Done daily. Together they train the front, the sides and the back of the trunk while keeping the spine in its neutral, comfortable position.

Modified curl-up

Hold 10 seconds; 6 reps, then 4, then 2 (rest ~20 s between sets)
McGill Big 3

Trains the front of the trunk without repeatedly bending the spine — which is the entire reason we do not use sit-ups.

  1. Lie on your back. Bend one knee with that foot flat on the floor; leave the other leg straight.
  2. Slide both hands, palms down, under the small of your back to support its natural hollow. Do not let your back flatten onto your hands.
  3. Brace your abdominal wall as you practised.
  4. Lift your head and shoulders only a centimetre or two off the floor — the head and neck ride with the chest as one rigid unit, as if head, neck and upper chest were in a plaster cast. Your chin does not tuck to your chest and your low back does not move.
  5. Hold for 10 seconds, breathing normally, then lower.
  6. Do 6 holds, rest, 4 holds, rest, 2 holds. Swap which knee is bent halfway through your sets.
Make it harderOnce 6-4-2 is easy, add a set (8-6-4), or lift the elbows a centimetre off the floor during the hold.
Make it easierDo not lift the head at all — simply brace and press the head lightly back into the floor for 10 seconds.
SafetyIf you get neck pain, you are lifting with your neck instead of your trunk. Lift less, and think of the whole upper body rising as one block.
Why it worksShort 8–10 second holds in a descending pyramid build the muscular endurance that distinguishes healthy backs from painful ones, without the repeated flexion cycles that damage discs in laboratory testing.

Side bridge (side plank)

Hold 10 seconds; 6 reps, then 4, then 2, each side
McGill Big 3

Trains the sides of the trunk — the muscles that stop you collapsing sideways — with very low compressive load on the spine.

  1. Lie on your side with your knees bent to about 90°, propped on the elbow directly under your shoulder, forearm flat.
  2. Place your top hand on the opposite shoulder.
  3. Brace, then lift your hips off the floor so your body makes a straight line from knees to shoulders.
  4. Hold 10 seconds, breathing normally, then lower.
  5. Do 6, 4, then 2 holds on that side, then roll over and repeat.
Make it harderStraighten the legs and support on your feet instead of your knees. Then, from the full position, roll slowly forwards and backwards a few degrees while staying stiff.
Make it easierKeep the hips on the floor and simply hold the propped-up position with a brace. Or do it standing, leaning your forearm on a wall and pushing your hip in towards it.
SafetyPainful shoulder is the usual limiter — do the wall version instead. Do not let the bottom shoulder sag.
Why it worksThe side bridge produces high activity in the lateral trunk muscles while keeping spinal compression far lower than sit-ups, which is why it is preferred for painful backs.

Bird dog

Hold 10 seconds; 6 reps, then 4, then 2, each side
McGill Big 3

Trains the muscles along the back of the spine and teaches you to move an arm and a leg while the spine stays still — the pattern you need for lifting, gardening and vacuuming.

  1. Kneel on all fours, hands under shoulders, knees under hips. Use a mat or folded towel under the knees.
  2. Brace your abdominal wall and set your back in its natural, neutral position — not arched up, not sagged down.
  3. Slide one arm forward along the floor and the opposite leg back, then lift both just to the height of your body. No higher: hips and shoulders stay square and level, as though balancing a cup of tea on your low back.
  4. Make a fist and reach it away, and push your heel away, as if pushing two walls apart. Hold 10 seconds while breathing.
  5. Return to all fours, sweep the hand and knee under you to touch briefly, then repeat.
  6. Do 6, 4, then 2 holds, then swap sides.
Make it harderDraw a small square in the air with the raised hand and the raised foot while the trunk stays completely still.
Make it easierLift the arm only, then the leg only, before combining them.
SafetySore wrists — make a fist and rest on your knuckles, or do it with forearms on a bench. Do not lift the leg high enough to arch your back.
Why it worksBird dog loads the spinal extensors while keeping the spine in a neutral, low-stress position, which is the recurring principle in every exercise on this page.
Why 10 seconds, and why 6 then 4 then 2?

Muscle endurance is built by repeated short contractions with brief rests, not by one long, grinding hold. Ten seconds is roughly the point at which a muscle's oxygen supply starts to be squeezed, so holding much longer trains fatigue rather than endurance. Descending the repetitions — six holds, then four, then two — lets you keep the quality high as you tire, which is exactly what you cannot do in a single two-minute plank.

Step 3 — Useful additions

Add these once the Big 3 are comfortable. They cover the hips, and they take the training into standing.

Dead bug

8–10 slow repetitions each side, 2 sets
Anti-arching control

Teaches you to keep your low back still while your arms and legs move — the same skill as bird dog, trained lying down where it is easier to control.

  1. Lie on your back, knees bent up over your hips, arms pointing at the ceiling.
  2. Brace lightly. Your low back keeps its small natural hollow — a hand slid underneath should feel light, steady pressure that does not change.
  3. Slowly lower one arm overhead and straighten the opposite leg towards the floor, going only as far as you can go without the pressure under your back changing.
  4. Breathe out as you extend, and bring them back slowly.
  5. Alternate sides. Stop the set as soon as the low back starts to arch.
Make it harderTake the leg lower and closer to the floor; slow the movement to a four-second count each way.
Make it easierMove one limb at a time; keep the moving leg bent and just slide the heel along the floor.
SafetyIf your back arches or your neck strains, you have gone too far — shorten the range.
Why it worksMotor-control exercises like this reduce pain and disability in chronic low back pain, though they are not clearly better than other well-delivered exercise. The best programme remains the one you will actually do.

Glute bridge

10 repetitions with a 5-second hold, 2 sets
Hip strength

Strengthens the buttock muscles, which take load off the low back when you stand, lift and climb stairs. Weak buttocks means an overworked back.

  1. Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat and hip-width apart, arms by your sides.
  2. Brace gently, then squeeze your buttocks and lift your hips until your body makes a straight line from knees to shoulders.
  3. The lift comes from squeezing the buttocks, not from arching the low back — you should feel it behind, not in the spine.
  4. Hold 5 seconds, then lower slowly.
  5. Repeat 10 times.
Make it harderHold longer (10 seconds), then march slowly on the spot at the top, then do it with one foot lightly off the floor.
Make it easierLift only halfway; or simply squeeze the buttocks hard for 5 seconds without lifting.
SafetyHamstring cramp is common — move your feet slightly further from your bottom and squeeze the buttocks harder.
Why it worksHip extensor strength is consistently reduced in people with persistent low back pain, and hip strengthening is a standard part of effective back programmes.

Standing anti-twist press

5 × 10-second holds each side
Standing carry-over

The most useful core work is done standing up. This trains your trunk to resist being twisted — exactly what happens when you carry shopping on one side or open a heavy door.

  1. Stand about half a metre from a wall, side-on, feet hip-width apart.
  2. Put both hands together, palms flat, against the wall at chest height, arms straight out in front of you.
  3. Brace your trunk, and press your hands into the wall as if trying to push it away. The wall will try to twist you — do not let it.
  4. Keep your hips and shoulders square and your trunk absolutely still. Breathe normally.
  5. Hold 10 seconds, rest, and do five holds before turning around to face the other way.
Make it harderStand in a narrow stance, then in a split stance, then press harder.
Make it easierStand closer to the wall and press more gently.
SafetyKeep breathing. If you feel it in your shoulder rather than your trunk, lower your hands slightly.
Why it worksTrunk stiffness generated while standing is what actually protects the spine during daily tasks; floor exercises alone do not automatically transfer.

Front plank (optional)

3 holds of 10–20 seconds
Optional add-on

A whole-trunk isometric hold. Useful, but not essential — the Big 3 cover the same ground with less shoulder and back strain.

  1. Rest on your forearms and knees, elbows under your shoulders.
  2. Brace, and lift your knees so your body makes a straight line from knees or feet to shoulders.
  3. Squeeze your buttocks, and do not let your hips sag or hike up.
  4. Hold 10–20 seconds with normal breathing, then rest. Three holds are plenty.
Make it harderFrom the knees to the toes; then lift one foot slightly for a few seconds at a time.
Make it easierDo it standing, with your forearms on the kitchen bench and your body angled forwards.
SafetyStop the moment your back begins to sag — a sagging plank loads exactly the structures we are protecting.
Why it worksLong plank holds are popular but there is no benefit in grinding out minutes: endurance for daily life is built with repeated short holds, not one exhausting one.

Step 4 — The part that matters most

No floor exercise beats simply moving regularly.

Walking as treatment for your back

20–30 minutes, most days
Strong evidence

Regular walking is one of the best-supported treatments for recurrent low back pain, and it is free.

  1. Start with what you can do comfortably, even if that is ten minutes.
  2. Increase by a few minutes each week rather than doubling it in one go.
  3. Walk at a comfortable, relaxed pace — this is not a fitness test.
  4. Expect some stiffness at first. Movement is safe; the back is a robust structure, and it does better with load than with rest.
  5. If pain flares after a walk, shorten the next one rather than stopping altogether.
Make it harderLonger, then slightly brisker; add gentle hills.
Make it easierThree short walks a day instead of one long one; walk in water if land walking is too painful.
SafetyBed rest is the one thing we now know makes back pain worse. Even during a flare, keep moving little and often.
Why it worksAn individually tailored, progressive walking programme substantially prolonged the time to a recurrence of low back pain in a large Australian randomised trial (the WalkBack trial, published in The Lancet in 2024).

A week of it

DailyThree days a weekEvery day
MorningGet up and move about for an hour before floor exercises—Walk
Main session (10–15 min)Curl-up 6/4/2 · side bridge 6/4/2 each side · bird dog 6/4/2 each sideAdd dead bug, glute bridge, anti-twist press—
Through the dayBrace before you lift, twist, or stand from a chair—Break up long sitting every 30–45 minutes

Ten to fifteen minutes a day. If you have time for only one thing, do the Big 3 — and walk.

The habits that decide whether it comes back

The exercises take fifteen minutes. What you do with the other fifteen hours matters more.

Hinge at the hips, do not curl the spine

To pick something up, push your bottom backwards and let your knees bend, keeping your back in its natural shape and your chest facing forwards. The movement happens at the hips.

For something light and low, the 'golfer's lift' is elegant and back-sparing: hold a chair or bench with one hand, tip forward at the hip and let the opposite leg swing back behind you like a see-saw.

Bring the load close before you lift it

The force through your low back depends far more on how far the load is from your body than on how heavy it is. A light box held at arm's length loads the spine more than a heavier one held against your chest. Step in close, brace, then lift.

Sitting is a position, not a punishment

There is no single correct sitting posture, and the evidence that posture causes back pain is much weaker than people are told. What does matter is duration: change position every half hour or so, and get up regularly. Use the chair's backrest, keep both feet on the floor, and support the small of your back with a rolled towel if that is comfortable.

Get out of bed in one piece

Roll onto your side with your knees bent, drop your feet over the edge of the bed, and push up with your arms so your trunk stays in one unit. Reverse it to get in. This is the single change that helps most people through a flare-up.

During a flare-up, keep moving little and often

Shorten your walks rather than stopping. Keep doing whatever exercises you can manage without a marked increase in pain. Use heat, use simple analgesia if you need it, and expect improvement over days to a few weeks.

Complete rest is the one approach that reliably makes things worse.

Things people are told that are not true

"My scan shows disc degeneration, so my back is damaged."

Degenerative changes, disc bulges and 'wear and tear' are found in large proportions of people with no pain at all, and they become more common with every decade — in the same way that grey hair does. They are usually a description of age rather than an explanation for pain.

There are important exceptions, which is what the red flags at the bottom of this page are for. But for most people, a scan report full of alarming words is not a reason to stop moving.

"I need to strengthen my core because it is weak."

Perhaps — but core weakness is not a proven cause of back pain, and stronger abdominal muscles have not been shown to prevent it. What exercise reliably does is reduce the pain and disability you have, and reduce recurrences. That is a good enough reason to do it. Be sceptical of anyone who tells you your pain is caused by one weak muscle.

"Motor control exercise is the best type of exercise for backs."

It works — but the reviews are clear that it is not clearly better than other well-delivered exercise, including general strengthening, Pilates, yoga and walking. The most important variable is whether you will keep doing it. If you hate these exercises, tell me, and we will choose something you will actually do.

"I should avoid bending forwards forever."

No. Avoiding a movement permanently makes it feel more threatening and makes the back less tolerant of it. The advice about bending applies to repeated, loaded bending, and to the first hour after getting up. The aim is to return to normal movement, gradually and confidently.

"Planks are the gold standard for core strength."

Long planks train endurance to fatigue and are hard on the shoulders and the low back once form fails. Short, repeated holds with good position beat one long hold, every time.

"Bed rest until it settles."

This was standard advice for decades and is now known to be actively harmful: it prolongs pain, weakens muscle, and increases the chance of the pain becoming persistent. Stay as active as the pain allows, and expect ordinary activity to be uncomfortable rather than damaging.

Making it actually happen

The best programme is the one you will still be doing in three months. These are the things that reliably make the difference.

🔗 Attach it to something you already do

Balance work while the kettle boils. Neck exercises after brushing your teeth. Relaxation practice as you get into bed. A new habit hooked onto an old one survives; a new habit floating free does not.

📅 Keep a tick sheet

A calendar on the fridge with a tick for each day. Self-monitoring is one of the few adherence strategies with consistent evidence behind it, and it gives us something real to look at in clinic.

🎯 Set a specific, checkable goal

Not 'improve my balance', but 'stand on one leg for 30 seconds each side by the end of March', or 'walk to the shops and back without stopping'. Write it down.

⏱️ Ten minutes beats an hour you never start

Short daily sessions beat one long weekly effort. The programmes below are designed to be done in ten to twenty minutes, most days, in your own kitchen or hallway.

Almost every trial that produced a real result ran for at least eight to twelve weeks. Judge the programme at three months, not at three days.

Getting extra help in Australia

You do not have to do this alone, and supervised programmes work better than unsupervised ones for people at higher risk.

🩺 Your GP can subsidise allied health

Under a GP Chronic Condition Management Plan (the successor to the old GP Management Plan / Team Care Arrangements), patients with a chronic condition can access a limited number of Medicare-rebated allied health sessions each calendar year — typically five in total, shared across all providers. Ask your GP whether you are eligible for physiotherapy or exercise physiology under this.

🏃 Physiotherapist or exercise physiologist

A physiotherapist is the right choice for a specific problem — a painful neck, an unsteady gait, vestibular rehabilitation. An accredited exercise physiologist is the right choice for building and supervising a long-term conditioning programme. Both can be seen privately without a referral.

👥 Community falls programmes

NSW Health and many local councils run group strength-and-balance programmes such as Stepping On. Group programmes add the two things a home sheet cannot: supervision and company. Ask your GP or your local council, or search Active and Healthy NSW.

🏠 My Aged Care and NDIS

If you are over 65 and finding daily tasks harder, a My Aged Care assessment can fund home exercise support, home modifications such as rails, and an occupational therapy home-safety visit. Under 65 with a permanent disability, the same supports may be available through the NDIS.

Stop and seek medical attention urgently if you develop
  • Loss of bladder or bowel control, difficulty passing urine, or numbness in the saddle area between the legs — this needs emergency assessment the same day.
  • Progressive weakness or numbness in a leg, or a foot that begins to drag.
  • Back pain with fever, unexplained weight loss, or night sweats.
  • Back pain following significant trauma, or in anyone with osteoporosis, long-term steroid use, or a history of cancer.
  • Severe pain that is worse at night and not relieved by lying down.
  • Morning back stiffness lasting more than an hour in a younger adult, improving with exercise and worsening with rest — this pattern suggests inflammatory back disease and needs a different assessment.
  • Pain that is simply not improving after six weeks of doing the right things.
